tagline: River, feeder canal and roadside mills trace a shared corridor
intro: The Delaware River Scenic Byway follows Route 29 between Frenchtown and the riverbank tunnel in Trenton. For much of the drive, both the Delaware and the Delaware and Raritan Feeder Canal are visible, with farm fields, forests and cliffs along the way. New Jersey DOT lists its historic, recreational and scenic qualities and gives its length as approximately 34 miles.

The road began as part of the Delaware River Drive legislated in 1911, a proposed state highway extending north from Trenton to the New York border. Route 29 initially turned toward Newark; the 1953 renumbering redirected it from Lambertville to Frenchtown over former Route 29A. In Trenton, freeway construction in the 1950s filled the old Trenton Water Power Canal, using its right of way for part of the highway. This corridor became the first New Jersey Scenic Byway in 1996 and gained national designation in 2009.

Travel south from Frenchtown through Raven Rock and Stockton to Lambertville, then Titusville and Washington Crossing State Park. North of the Scudder Falls Bridge interchange, River Road is a two-lane surface road beside the canal. Toward Trenton, the route becomes a mix of boulevard and expressway. The State Capitol is visible from Route 29 before the byway ends at the tunnel.
notice: Watch for the feeder canal between the highway and the Delaware River.

moments.title: Raven Rock
moments.text: The hamlet’s namesake rock outcrop marks the southwest corner of the Hunterdon Plateau. Bulls Island links two states by a steel suspension footbridge across the Delaware. The Lumberville–Raven Rock crossing connects the island with Lumberville, Pennsylvania; it carried road traffic from 1856 to 1944. Another transport route changed its purpose here too. Passenger trains served Raven Rock until 1952, and freight continued until the line closed in 1978. In the early 1980s, the railway right of way became a recreation trail. The D&R Canal Trail runs through the surrounding park on the former railroad bed.

moments.title: Prallsville Mills
moments.text: A grist mill from 1877 and a linseed oil mill from 1790 are among the buildings at Prallsville Mills. The feeder canal reached the community in the 1830s, followed by the Belvidere-Delaware Railroad along the canal in the 1850s. The property became part of the state park in 1973. When New Jersey could not fund restoration, local residents formed the Delaware River Mill Society in 1976. The society remains responsible for restoring, maintaining and operating the mill complex and John Prall Jr. House. The mill district now serves as an open-air museum within Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park.

moments.title: Washington Crossing State Park
moments.text: Johnson's Ferry was the New Jersey landing for Washington and 2,400 Continental Army soldiers crossing the Delaware overnight on December 25–26, 1776. Across the Delaware, the corresponding Pennsylvania landing was known as McConkey's Ferry. They were preparing a surprise attack on Trenton. The Johnson Ferry House was both an 18th-century farmhouse and tavern, owned by ferry operator Garret Johnson. Several rooms contain period furnishings, and an 18th-century kitchen garden has been planted. The park museum follows the campaign through the battles of Trenton, Assunpink Creek and Princeton, with a collection of American and British military artifacts.
